Density of the Modified Half-Normal Distribution

Source: R/dmhn.R
dmhn.Rd

Computes the probability density function (or log-density) of the Modified Half-Normal (MHN) distribution with parameters alpha, beta, and gamma.

Usage

dmhn(x, alpha = 1, beta = 1, gamma = 0, log = FALSE)

Arguments

x

Numeric vector of evaluation points.

alpha

Shape parameter (\(\alpha > 0\)). Scalar or numeric vector. Default: 1.

beta

Rate-type parameter (\(\beta > 0\)), the coefficient of the Gaussian tail \(\exp(-\beta x^2)\); larger values pull mass toward zero. Scalar or numeric vector. Default: 1.

gamma

Tilt parameter (\(\gamma \in R\)), the coefficient of the exponential tilt \(\exp(\gamma x)\). Scalar or numeric vector. Default: 0.

log

Logical; if TRUE, log-density is returned. Default: FALSE. Read with as.logical(), so that 1 is TRUE; a value that gives NA is an error.

Value

A numeric vector. The output length equals max(length(x), length(alpha), length(beta), length(gamma)), or 0 if any of them has length zero; each input is recycled to that length following standard R recycling rules. For x < 0, the density is 0 (-Inf if log = TRUE). At x = 0 it is Inf for alpha < 1, the truncated normal density at 0 for alpha = 1 (\(2\sqrt{\beta/\pi}\) at gamma = 0), and 0 for alpha > 1. As in dgamma, an element whose parameters lie outside the parameter space (alpha or beta not positive and finite, or gamma not finite) is NaN, with a warning, and an element with an NA or NaN among its inputs is NA or NaN (NA if any of them is NA), without one; the other elements are unaffected. The arguments must be numeric (double, integer or logical): a factor, a character string, a complex number, a list or NULL is an error, as in dnorm. As with dnorm, the attributes of x (names, dim, dimnames) are kept when the result has the length of x; a classed x, such as a Date, is taken as its numbers and gives a plain vector. Unlike dnorm, attributes of a longer parameter vector are not carried over.

Details

The MHN density (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 1a) is $$f(x \mid \alpha, \beta, \gamma) = \frac{2 \beta^{\alpha/2} x^{\alpha-1} \exp(-\beta x^2 + \gamma x)}{\Psi[\alpha/2, \gamma/\sqrt{\beta}]} \quad (x > 0)$$ where \(\Psi[a, z] = \sum_{n \ge 0} \Gamma(a + n/2) z^n / n!\) is the Fox-Wright function \({}_1\Psi_1[(a, 1/2); (1, 0); z]\) (Sun et al. 2023, Supplementary Eq. (1)).

The default parameters alpha = 1, beta = 1, gamma = 0 correspond to the half-normal distribution \(\mathrm{HN}(1/\sqrt{2})\).

At \(\gamma = 0\) and at \(\alpha = 1\) exactly the density is computed from the closed form of the law it reduces to; a shape or a tilt merely close to those values is a different law, and is computed as in the general case:

  • \(\gamma = 0\): sqrt-Gamma distribution, for \(\alpha \le 10^6\). Above it the Gamma law of \(\beta X^2\) is so narrow that rounding \(\beta x^2\) moves it by a visible part of its width (up to about \(10^{-5}\) of the log density at \(\alpha = 10^{20}\)), and \(\gamma = 0\) is measured from the peak as below.

  • \(\alpha = 1\): truncated normal distribution (Sun et al., 2023, Lemma 6b), the normal law of mean \(\mu = \gamma/(2\beta)\) and standard deviation \(\sigma = 1/\sqrt{2\beta}\) restricted to \((0, \infty)\): dnorm divided by its upper tail at 0 where 0 lies within 1000 standard deviations of the mean (\(|\gamma|/\sqrt{2\beta} \le 1000\)). Farther out the same ratio is written with the normal hazard where 0 lies above the mean, so that two logarithms of about \(-\gamma^2/(4\beta)\) are not subtracted, and from the standardised point \((x - \mu)/\sigma\), formed directly, where it lies below. Where \(\gamma/(2\beta)\) passes the largest double under a negative tilt, the density is the exponential one, \(-\gamma e^{\gamma x}\).

A subnormal shape, below the smallest normal double \(2.2 \times 10^{-308}\), is computed apart, at \(\gamma = 0\) too. There half of \(\alpha\) is not always a double and \(1/\alpha\) can overflow, while \(t^\alpha = 1\) to double precision at every positive double \(t\); the density is then \(\alpha e^{-\beta x^2 + \gamma x} / (x (1 + w))\), with \(w = \alpha K_0(z)\) and \(K_0(z) = \int_0^1 (e^{-t^2 + z t} - 1) / t \, dt + \int_1^\infty e^{-t^2 + z t} / t \, dt\). \(1 / (1 + w)\) is the probability that \(X\) lies below the smallest positive double. Below a tilt of about 52 (53 at the smallest shapes) it is 1 in double precision: pmhn is 1 at every positive \(x\), qmhn is 0 for every lower-tail probability below 1 given on the probability scale (the upper tail, or log.p = TRUE, still gives the quantiles of the far upper tail), and rmhn returns 0. For a large tilt \(w\) is the mass at the peak of the kernel against the mass by the origin; it is below \(10^{-200}\) in size for \(z \le 30\), and negative below \(z\) of about 0.3. pmhn, qmhn, rmhn and the moment functions take the same form. It serves the whole law up to a tilt between about 55 and 56.3, as \(\alpha\) falls. Above it the mass by the origin is at most \(2^{-64}\), about \(5.4 \times 10^{-20}\), of the whole, and the density, the upper tail, the moments and the law of the draws no longer depend on \(\alpha\); the lower tail far below the peak, of which that mass is more than \(2^{-64}\), is still taken from the same form up to where it reaches one half.

Computation is performed in log-space to avoid numerical underflow/overflow. For a shape \(\alpha\) or a scale-free tilt \(z = \gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\) above \(10^6\), and wherever the terms of the ordinary form grow too large (see Range), the log density is measured instead from the peak \(v^*\) of the density of \(\log X\), the positive root of \(2\beta x^2 - \gamma x - \alpha = 0\), as \((\alpha - 1)(\log(1+\rho) - \rho) - \rho - \beta d^2\) less the logarithm of \(v^*\) times the peak-normalised integral of the law, with \(d = x - v^*\) and \(\rho = d/v^*\). The ordinary form adds terms of size \(\alpha \log x\) and \((\alpha/2) \log\beta\), and for \(z > 10^3\) measures x from the centre \(\gamma/(2\beta)\) rounded to a double; their rounding passes \(10^{-7}\) at \(\alpha = 10^8\), and \(10^{-6}\) at \(z = 10^{10}\) unless \(\beta\) is a power of 2. Here neither is formed, and \(d\) is exact: \(v^*\) is held as a double next to it plus its offset from that double.

Range. The ordinary form is used only while the larger \(m\) of \(\alpha\) and \(z\) is at most \(10^6\) and \(m (1 + |\log v^*|)\), the size of its largest terms, is at most \(10^7\): at \(\beta = 1\) up to a shape of \(10^6\) or a tilt of about \(7.3 \times 10^5\), and at \(\beta = 10^{\pm 300}\) up to about \(3 \times 10^4\) for either. That keeps its rounding to about \(2 \times 10^{-9}\); measured from the peak the error is about \(10^{-12}\), relative to the size of the log density where that is large. So for \(\alpha \le 10^{15}\), \(|z| \le 10^{15}\) and \(\beta\) in \([10^{-300}, 10^{300}]\) the log density is accurate to the working tolerance sqrt(.Machine$double.eps). Outside that range the law can be narrower than the spacing of the doubles near its peak (for \(z\) above about \(10^{16}\), or \(\alpha\) above about \(10^{31}\)), and the density is still that of the exact law at the double x given, almost always 0 there. For a positive tilt whose mode \(\gamma/(2\beta)\) lies beyond the largest double, which needs a subnormal \(\beta\), log = TRUE returns -Inf where the log density is finite. Two cases give NA with a warning instead: within 45 standard deviations of the peak of a law narrower than the spacing by a factor of order \(10^{19}\) (\(z\) beyond about \(10^{35}\), \(\alpha\) beyond about \(10^{70}\)), where the position of the peak cannot be resolved finely enough; and where the whole law lies beyond the largest double without a positive tilt to place it (a shape near the largest double against a subnormal \(\beta\)). Where \(z\) itself overflows, the law is its limit: Gamma(\(\alpha\), rate \(|\gamma|\)) under a negative tilt and normal about its mode with variance \(1/(2\beta)\) under a positive one. For \(\alpha = 1\) and a truncation point \(z_0 = -\gamma/\sqrt{2\beta}\) beyond \(10^3\) the truncated-normal density is written with the normal hazard \(\phi(z_0)/\bar\Phi(z_0)\), and below \(-10^3\) with the offset \(2\beta x - \gamma\) formed in one rounding (as \(\beta x - \gamma/2\), so also where \(2\beta\) overflows), so that it holds to the Exponential and normal limits it tends to.

When any of alpha, beta, gamma is a vector, the density is evaluated element-wise. The Fox-Wright \(\Psi\) normalizing constant is computed once for each position of the recycling cycle while that cycle is at most 256 long, and otherwise once for each run of consecutive elements that share the \((\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\) triple. So recycled parameters, and parameter vectors in which equal triples are adjacent, are much faster than triples that alternate along a long vector, and than calling dmhn inside an R loop.

References

Sun, J., Kong, M., & Pal, S. (2023). The Modified-Half-Normal distribution: Properties and an efficient sampling scheme. Communications in Statistics - Theory and Methods, 52(5), 1591–1613.

See also

mhn_mean, mhn_var, mhn_mode

Examples

x <- seq(0, 5, length.out = 100)
plot(x, dmhn(x, alpha = 2, beta = 1, gamma = 1), type = "l")


# Log-density
dmhn(1, alpha = 2, beta = 1, gamma = 1, log = TRUE)
#> [1] -0.3112403
